item.title: Texas vs Ohio State is more than a rematch: A BBQ-fueled collision between college football power brokers
item.description: Ohio State fans spent $22,000 on an AirBnB and another $3,000 on tickets for the Buckeyes' trek to Austin, where Texas awaits in a Top-5 rematch.
item.content:encoded:
The anticipation has been brewing since last year's dud of a game in Columbus. The rematch is set for Saturday night in Texas, as Ohio State makes the 1,234 mile trek to Austin for a rematch with the Longhorns.

But more importantly, Steve Sarkisian will have his 'semifinals aren’t good enough' mantra tested by a Buckeyes team looking to make another Big Ten statement in what is now "SEC Country."

While the offseason has been filled with questions surrounding whether this is the year Arch Manning takes the next step in becoming one of the best quarterbacks to come out of Austin, the bigger question is whether both Texas and Ohio State can justify spending over $40 million on their 2026 roster.

LSU PRESIDENT WADE ROUSSE ENDS LANE KIFFIN'S SEC SHOWDOWN, BUT THERE IS STILL RELATIONSHIPS TO MEND

In reality, the storylines write themselves when it comes to what happens on the field. Will this turn into a shootout in Austin, or will both defenses rise to the occasion to limit both Manning and Julian Sayin?

Either way, we're in for a show on Saturday night.

And, there will be thousands of Ohio State fans in town to witness the next chapter of this convenient rivalry. It didn’t take very long for the first Buckeyes to be seen, at least by me, on their way to Austin for this Top-5 showdown.

Sitting at the gate inside the Nashville airport, waiting to board my flight to Austin, the trash talking had already begun.

"Look, I know you're headed to Austin, but I just wanted to tell you all 'Go Buckeyes' and I hope the ride back is a bit longer," a Southwest gate agent said over the intercom.

What more could you ask for? Trash talking by the guy who is scanning our plane tickets is the perfect way to get this weekend started.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

In all honesty, the more entertaining part came on the actual plane. Sitting two-seats over from a fan donning an Ohio State pullover, the Buckeye started explaining how much it was costing him for this college football adventure that would have him meeting up with four of his friends a little later than expected, thanks to a three-hour delay in the Music City.

How much was this Airbnb that would become their Buckeye fortress over the next three days?

"In all, it was around $22,000 for the entire house," the Ohio State fan told me while sitting in the 23rd row of a Southwest airline flight. "Add on another $3,000 for tickets, and we darn sure better be headed home with a win."

He was only half-kidding, most likely questioning his financial decisions if Ohio State left Texas with a loss, or somehow the ridiculously expensive housing turned into a nightmare. I will say, judging by the rentals I then had to look up on the site following his oddly truthful explanation of expenditures, his group would at least have a nice Alaska king to sleep on over these next three days.

I'll enjoy my sleep at the $237 a night hotel that the company luckily procured through some fantastic booking tactics on my part.

Think of the party scene in this town as a tamed Bourbon Street, though I did my best to stay away from the raucous environment that I was told was coming after the 11 p.m. CT hour on both nights.

Sorry, I'm at the age where the body starts shutting down around 8 p.m., and my brain had already hit a wall around two hours earlier. I just can't keep up with these kids nowadays, and I have zero shame in admitting that.

But, from the bustling music to the strong smell of marijuana pumping from the streets, it was pretty obvious as to why this town is such a tourist attraction. The restaurants were one of a kind, though we usually don't give out free advertisements around here.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Though, you don't come to Texas without trying some of this BBQ that would make you wanna slap your mama. No, don't hit your mom, it's just a phrase us southerners use when describing a stellar food choice.

There had to be a stop at Terry Black's BBQ, where we were joined by a plethora of Ohio State fans who had made the trip to Austin. Some of them must have came straight from the airport, carrying their luggage into the local establishment, which is also known as a BBQ cathedral.

But, past all of the love of pork and ribs, the distaste for their opponents wasn’t hard to find. That even included the 'team up north', according to a few Buckeyes.

"F--- Michigan," one Ohio State fan yelled through the sweet haze of BBQ smoke.

It certainly doesn’t get much bigger than this, especially for an early season game.

Arch Manning versus Julian Sayin.

Jeremiah Smith on one side, Cam Coleman on the other.

A Texas defense looking to create its own noise versus an Ohio State offense, that are both talented enough to help each team play for a national championship.

For an entire year, we've waited on this rematch in Austin. We all know that both squads have spent the money needed to field a championship-winning team. Now, it's time to prove it on the field, with over 100,000 fans watching inside DKR Stadium, and millions tuning in at home.

It's the Longhorns vs. the Buckeyes. The SEC versus the Big Ten.

We are in for a show tonight in Texas, with plenty of college football fans wondering if Arch Manning can take the next step in this journey to have fans proclaim 'Texas Is Back'.

Obviously, we've got a long way to go in the 2026 season, but tonight we see just how good each one of these contenders really are.

Or, maybe we leave Austin with one team looking like a pretender.

Either way, the BBQ was delightful.

item.content:encoded:

The good news is that I have plenty of weeks to dig myself out of the hole I built, but the bad news is that it happened at all. Today, I have a play for this match between Alabama and Kentucky.

Alabama is one of those schools that is synonymous with College Football. They haven’t been at the top of the nation in a few years, but they are still a tough team with plenty of talent. They started their season with a strong victory over East Carolina University. They won 48-10 with very little struggle to get things going. It was a good sign for a team looking to adjust to Keelon Russell being under center full time.

Russell looked great in his first game this season, even if he wasn’t all that accurate with his throws. Perhaps that is something to watch over the next few games. The Alabama quarterback threw 30 times and only completed 18 of his passes. He did run 13 times for 86 yards and a touchdown. The ground game was strong for Alabama in this one, so Russell also didn’t need to be overly accurate. They ran the ball 49 times for 227 yards and five touchdowns.

Kentucky also opened their season with a rather inferior opponent. They faced the Youngstown State Penguins and blew them out 45-13. It was actually a bit of a surprise that they allowed 13 points to their opponent, and not all of it was in garbage time. The story of this game was really not about the Wildcats' defense; it was about how good the offense looked in their first game. item.title: Texas Longhorns seek revenge against top-ranked Ohio State after last season's seven-point loss
item.description: College football's top-ranked Ohio State visits Texas after Julian Sayin threw for 320 yards in the opener but managed just 126 against Texas.
item.content:encoded:
As much fun as College Football is, even I have to admit that most of the teams are, well, scared at the beginning of the season. Sure, these games between obscure schools and powerhouses get some excitement for the random school, and money coming into them.

As far as watching, it is kind of boring seeing a team win games by 40 points. I want to see ranked matchups early on – if we have expanded playoffs, teams should be forced to play tougher games to start their year. It means the regular season is actually meaningful and that if a team does go undefeated, they’ve been challenged. If Notre Dame goes undefeated, we will look at maybe two games this year and be impressed. However, if you have teams like Ohio State and Texas facing each other early in the year, and throughout the season, and one goes undefeated, it is much more impressive.

Ohio State comes in as the top-ranked team in the country. The Buckeyes looked every bit of it in their season opener as they dominated Ball State with a 56-3 victory. Ohio State looked great on offense, with an extremely efficient Julian Sayin throwing for 320 yards on 21 of 25 passes with three touchdowns. Even both of his backups were solid, both going 5-for-6 with over 50 yards and a touchdown. This wasn’t exactly a challenging game for the team.

Ohio State now needs to figure out how to beat a Texas defense that is one of the better in the nation. It will be a good challenge after last year’s battle the two teams had. Ohio State looked great in basically every game last year, but scored only 14 against the Longhorns last season. Sayin had only 126 passing yards in that game, the fewest of the entire season.

Texas enters today’s game as the fourth-ranked team in the nation, and once again has high expectations. Those expectations will be tested early in the season, just as they were last year. In 2025, Texas had to travel to Ohio State for the first game of the season. They put up a respectable fight, but the offense got very little going in that one, with just seven points. Arch Manning looked very uncomfortable under center, completing just over 50% of his passes for 170 yards, one touchdown, and one interception.

The Longhorns had a different start this season with an easy win over Texas State. I was wrong about this game, as I expected Texas to take its foot off the gas. The Longhorns somewhat did, scoring just 10 points in the final quarter and taking Manning out in the third, but they had too many points already to keep the under in play. Manning looked much better in this game with 305 yards, four touchdowns, and completing 20 of 27 passes. He did have an interception, though.

item.title: El-Sayed’s ISNA appearance draws scrutiny over controversial speakers
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed appeared on an ISNA panel with Cenk Uygur and Zaid Shakir days before the 9/11 anniversary, raising new questions about his campaign.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is facing questions about his appearance at an Islamic Society of North America (ISNA) convention after the organization removed a Pakistani cleric from its lineup following scrutiny of his past remarks about Hitler, Jews and jihad.

Mufti Tariq Masood had been scheduled to speak at ISNA's annual convention last week in Detroit alongside El-Sayed. The Washington Free Beacon first reported that ISNA had quietly pulled Masood from its list of speakers last month. This came after his past comments, including remarks appearing to praise Hitler's persecution of the Jews and defending child marriage, sparked backlash against ISNA.

Dr. Andrew Bostom, who reviewed one of Masood's sermons, told Fox News Digital that the cleric "basically said that the Quran had foreshadowed Hitler 1,400 years ago."

FATWAS, HOLY WARS AND SOCIALISM: INSIDE THE ISLAMIC CONFERENCE WHERE EL-SAYED DREW A HERO’S WELCOME

Bostom said that Masood's remarks should not be looked at in isolation, but rather within a larger pattern of antisemitic themes that have appeared in writings of some Muslim scholars. He cited Muhammad Sayyid Tantawy, the late Grand Imam of Al-Azhar University in Egypt, who he said was "the near papal equivalent for Sunni Islam," in terms of his influence.

The controversy over Masood prompted the Zionist Organization of America (ZOA) to ask Secretary of State Marco Rubio to deny or review any visa issued to the cleric.

"Masood is a racist, Jew-hate-mongering, anti-American, anti-British, conspiracy-promoting, murder- and terror-inciter. Masood even praises Hitler’s genocide of Jews as doing the right thing, similar to the Quran’s instructions," ZOA National President Morton Klein wrote in his Aug. 19 letter to Rubio.

At the time, Bostom said it was unclear whether Masood had already entered the U.S. or still planned to attend the convention, even if he had been removed from the list of speakers.

TIM SCOTT GOES SCORCHED EARTH ON EL-SAYED: 'HE'S FOR HAMAS, BUT HE'S AGAINST AMERICA'

While Masood ultimately did not speak at the convention, his removal from the lineup did not resolve questions about the event's speakers or El-Sayed's decision to participate.

At the conference, El-Sayed appeared on a panel with far-left Young Turks founder Cenk Uygur and controversial New Jersey-based cleric Zaid Shakir, according to ISNA's itinerary. The panel was titled "Cultivating God Awareness in a Turmoiled America." In the description of the panel, ISNA said the session was aimed at turning taqwa, which means God-Awareness, "into actionable guidance, equipping participants not merely to survive but thrive in workplaces, schools, digital spaces, and community life, and to succeed on their own terms."

CBS CHIEF BARI WEISS' INVOLVEMENT IN VIRAL EL-SAYED REPORT SPARKS DEBATE AMONG CRITICS

Neither Uygur nor Shakir are strangers to controversy. In February, Uygur wrote on X that "I no longer believe the official 9/11 story." Uygur said that those who would be outraged by his statement had been "brainwashed by corporate media."

Shakir has described himself as "extremely anti-American," according to The Washington Free Beacon. The outlet also reported that in 1992, Shakir urged Muslims to embrace "extrasystemic political action," including "noncooperation tactics to guerrilla war" to influence government policies.

The ISNA conference took place just days before the 25th anniversary of 9/11, making Uygur and Shakir's presence, and El-Sayed's participation, all the more notable. El-Sayed faced his own 9/11 controversy earlier this week over now-deleted tweets from 2021 in which he said he mourned the lives lost in the attacks before taking a swipe at America, according to The New York Post.

"Today, I mourn the 3K lives, 6K injuries, & infrastructural devastation in NYC, perpetrated ignorantly in the name of my faith. Tomorrow, I’ll mourn ~1M lives, millions of injuries, & infrastructural devastation in 3 countries, perpetrated ignorantly in the name of my country," El-Sayed wrote on Sept. 11, 2021.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

While addressing the ISNA conference, El-Sayed reportedly focused on anti-Muslim hate, according to the Post.

"We found ourselves in a moment now where, as people point to us, Muslim Americans, they want to tell us that we don’t belong," El-Sayed said, according to the Post.

"They want to tell us that this country is not ours. They want to tell us that because of our names or how we pray, that somehow we are less than," he added.

El-Sayed previously faced scrutiny for campaigning alongside controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who is Uygur's nephew. Piker was criticized back in 2019 for saying that "America deserved 9/11." He later apologized and retracted the statement. El-Sayed has offered criticism of some of Piker's remarks but has yet to fully disavow him.

Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed and ISNA for comment.

item.title: The universe’s beautiful fine-tuning leaves atheism facing its biggest question
item.description: A Getty Museum visit with Leonardo da Vinci's art sparked a former atheist's journey into the anthropic principle and our fine-tuned universe.
item.content:encoded:
Years ago, at Los Angeles’ Getty Museum, I was given the rare privilege of a personal, after-hours tour of Leonardo da Vinci’s artwork. Standing alone in the quiet, dimly lit gallery, mere inches from a sepia-colored sketch of a human face composed of several dozen perfectly placed wavy lines, I knew without a doubt I was in the presence of pure genius.

After years of being an atheist for whom science was god and the cosmos was a miraculous accident, I now know with equal certainty our universe, too, is a work of pure genius.

Why is that?

'MILESTONE': SCIENTISTS CLAIM TO BUILD SYNTHETIC CELL, RAISING CONCERNS IN STEP TOWARD ARTIFICIAL LIFE

In 1973, scientists from around the world gathered in Kraków, Poland, to celebrate the 500th birthday of Nicolaus Copernicus. Part of the conference concerned a fifty-year-old unsolved mystery called the "large-number coincidences." The numerical values of natural phenomena large and small – the radius of the observable universe, the charge of an electron, the strength of gravity, and so forth – follow a pattern hard to dismiss as mere coincidence.

What could possibly explain this?

METEORITE THAT CRASHED INTO NJ HOME HOLDS BUILDING BLOCKS OF LIFE, SCIENTISTS SAY

Australian physicist Brandon Carter stood before the August gathering and offered a provocative observation that came to be called the Anthropic Principle. The special numerical "coincidences," he said, are inexorably linked to the one thing that makes our universe special: we and our fellow lifeforms. Without life, the universe would be an unremarkable ghost town.

Carter’s presentation ignited the explosive birth of a brand-new science dedicated to fully answering the fifty-year-old mystery: Is it mere coincidence our universe has just the right numerical composition for life to be possible — especially life as complex as humans — or is there more to it than that?

SCIENTISTS REVIVE ANCIENT 24,000-YEAR-OLD ‘ZOMBIE WORM’ FROM ARCTIC ICE — THEN IT REPRODUCED

Think of when you get your annual physical. The nurse measures your four core vital signs — body temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate — which yield a pattern of numbers that reveals important information about your insides.

The universe’s numerical profile serves the same purpose: it tells us something essential about the inner being of the cosmos. And what it tells us, after decades of careful examination involving increasingly precise astronomical observations, laboratory experiments, and theoretical calculations, is that our universe is not merely a coincidence. Far from it.

"I find it quite improbable that such order came out of chaos," stated the late American cosmologist and former atheist Allan Sandage. "There has to be some organizing principle."

COULD NOAH'S ARK REMAINS BE BURIED IN TURKEY? NEW FINDINGS REVIVE AGE-OLD DEBATE

British astronomer Sir Fred Hoyle, whom I had the honor of getting to know as a grad student at Cornell, concurred: "A commonsense interpretation of the facts suggests that a super-intellect has monkeyed with physics … and that there are no blind forces worth speaking about in nature. The numbers one calculates from the facts seem to me so overwhelming as to put this conclusion almost beyond question."

This startling revelation does not set well with atheists, who twist themselves into knots trying to defend the belief that everything — life and all — is but a happy accident, courtesy of purposeless laws of nature. The problem they have is explaining where those supposedly blind natural agents came from.

Another valiant attempt to rescue the naturalistic worldview is the multiverse hypothesis. If there are an infinite number of universes, then it is no surprise at least one of them — ours — is tailor-made for life.

But many decades of seeking ways to test this fantastic idea have failed. That’s because parallel universes are in principle isolated from one another and therefore beyond the reach of our observations.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

"The idea that we live in a multiverse is a fringe idea in a small part of a subfield of the physics community," says German theoretical physicist Sabine Hossenfelder. "Nobody who does serious science works with the multiverse because it’s utterly useless."

So, then, we all now face this burning question screaming for an answer: If our universe is not a coincidence, how do we explain it?

AMERICA ISN’T DONE WITH JESUS — AND THE BESTSELLER LIST JUST PROVED IT

For me, the answer goes back to that unforgettable day at the Getty. As I stood there, seized by the ineffable beauty of Leonardo da Vinci’s exquisite sketch, it never would have occurred to me to entertain the notion that it was an accident.

Today, likewise, when I contemplate life, the night sky, and the precision and improbability of the vital signs that define the essence of our cosmos, my reaction is crystal-clear and supported by the latest scientific evidence. In both the outer and inner being of the universe, I perceive not the throw of dice, but the hand of a Master Artist.

item.title: Political fights can rip couples apart — therapist shares 3 ways to save a relationship
item.description: A marriage therapist reveals three strategies for couples navigating the political divide, from setting boundaries to finding compromise.
item.content:encoded:
More than one-third of Americans report having ended a relationship over political differences, according to recent research – and experts say those divisions may also be straining some marriages.

Some high-profile couples, including Democratic strategist James Carville and his wife, Republican political consultant Mary Matalin, have remained together despite their differing views – but experts say navigating those differences isn't always easy.

Anna Elton, PhD, a licensed marriage and family therapist and clinical sexologist in Massachusetts, said she has counseled couples on different sides of the political aisle.

'QUIET QUITTING' COULD SILENTLY DESTROY YOUR MARRIAGE – 4 WAYS TO BRING THE SPARK BACK

"A lot of couples come in and they want to work on communication, and politics can come up in our sessions," Elton, author of "The Formula of Desire," told Fox News Digital.

"I work with a number of couples who are in this place where they have a family, they have kids, but they can't talk about politics."

For many singles, Elton said, political compatibility is now something they consider early in the dating process.

WHY COUPLES SHOULD FLIRT WITH EACH OTHER EVERY DAY – PLUS THE 'RED FLAG' TO AVOID

She referenced a recent study that found younger adults tend to make assumptions about religion, gender roles, empathy and other characteristics based on political affiliation.

"So, before you get to know the person, you’ve already created this assumption of who this person is."

"I've definitely been hearing from my younger clients who are saying, ‘I want to know which political party this person belongs to, and then I'll see if I want to even be going on a date and wasting my time with this person.’"

COMMON MARRIAGE HABIT COULD QUIETLY KILL YOUR SEX LIFE, EXPERT WARNS

For couples who have been married for decades, today's political divisions may present challenges that didn't exist when their relationships began, Elton noted.

The expert offered the following three tips for navigating politically charged conversations with a partner in a healthy way.

Come up with rules for the conversation and set the tone before it starts, Elton suggested, noting that the first three minutes of a discussion typically predict the outcome.

Conversations that begin with a harsh tone or accusatory language are unlikely to be productive, she said. "So, before you talk, say, ‘Okay, these are our boundaries for this conversation.’"

Those boundaries can also extend to media habits, Elton said, including limiting how much political content couples consume, especially on social media.

"You read certain things and then all of a sudden, you keep scrolling on your social media and you see similar content coming up over and over and over again," Elton said. "And at this point, it creates an illusionary effect."

HOW OFTEN ARE MARRIED PEOPLE HAVING SEX? WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT THE INTIMACY STANDARD IN AMERICA

Hearing the same information repeatedly may lead people to gradually accept it as true, according to Elton. "Now think about two people who are in their echo chambers, and they're exposed to certain information that is contradicting each other."

As a general rule, Elton said couples should be mindful not to spend more time on their phones than they do engaging with each other. Excessive screen time can reduce face-to-face connection, leaving less room for eye contact, conversation and other shared experiences.

Also, when someone is constantly consuming political content, it can become the primary topic they want to discuss, creating tension when partners hold different views, she cautioned.

To help reduce conflict, Elton recommended limiting when political news or posts are consumed. She also suggested setting aside one phone-free date night each week to encourage face-to-face connection.

While couples with differing political views are unlikely to agree on every issue, "agreeing to disagree" can help prevent hostility.

"We can still love each other," Elton said. "It's not going to affect our relationship."

"As soon as it gets to the point of seeing your partner through the lens of ‘if you believe this, this is who you are, and I can’t believe that I'm still in a relationship with you,’ that becomes a problem."

Elton urged couples not to take political disagreements personally and instead approach them with curiosity. She also recommended looking at the same information together, allowing each partner to ask questions and draw their own conclusions rather than jumping into a heated debate.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The therapist also encouraged couples to focus on areas of common ground rather than viewing disagreements in black-and-white terms.

After a disagreement or failure to compromise, it’s important to always reconnect with your partner, she emphasized.

Sharing reassuring words like "I love you" and "you matter to me more than anything else" can be helpful, she said.

"I feel like you always need to say, ‘Hey, I hear what you're saying, but I'm not agreeing, and that's okay.’"

When politics come into play in a relationship, it can have an impact on more than just the couple.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Elton encouraged partners to consider how sharing certain opinions can impact other loved ones, especially if one person confides in a family member or friend about the other's views.

"You can create this triangulation where you're connecting with someone against your partner, and you don't want that," she warned.

"Talk to your therapist, vent to your therapist … because if you start venting to your family and friends, then they start forming certain opinions about your partner, and it can affect how they talk to them, how they interact with them."

Before making any drastic decisions, such as ending a relationship over political discord, Elton suggested slowing down and returning to a more grounded state.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"We hear certain things and we fill in the gaps," she said. "When we hear someone's political affiliation, we often make assumptions about who they are without really hearing them out."

Rather than making assumptions based on the media or podcasts a partner consumes, for example, Elton encouraged couples to ask questions, stay curious and remain open-minded.

item.title: OutKick's Craig Carton reveals the real reason Nike stock is in the tank: 'They're failing miserably'
item.description: Craig Carton traces Nike's downfall from its Colin Kaepernick partnership to the Dylan Mulvaney sports bra campaign that replaced Brandi Chastain.
item.content:encoded:
In case you've been living under a rock these past few days, Nike has had a rough time this week.

Between the unveiling of their universally reviled "Specter Edition" NBA jerseys to their stock taking a nosedive, the company that was once seen as unsinkable is starting to take on water.

Things have gotten so bad for Nike that they're set to be booted from the S&P 100, a sign that the company is trending in the wrong direction.

OutKick's Craig Carton, a self-admitted "Nike man," thinks he knows what the issue is, and if you've been paying attention, it shouldn't come as a shock to you.

"This is part of the problem right here," Carton says as he points at a picture of the aforementioned Specter Edition jerseys. "Nike decided, apparently, to hire a blind creator to basically pull a Jackson Pollock and just start ramming paint at the wall."

If you've seen the jerseys, Carton is spot on.

I've likened them to a Windows screensaver from the 90s that has been ripped from a dying computer monitor, but Jackson Pollock is a solid pull as well.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"Part of the reason for Nike's downfall is garbage like this," he explains.

But, as Carton alludes to, it's only part of the problem. The other half of the issue is more historical.

"In 2018, Nike decided to get in bed with Colin Kaepernick," Carton recounts. "And they scrapped 'Just Do It' and they started a new slogan, which was 'Dream Crazy.'"

"The only thing crazy that they did was partner with a lunatic who hates America."

Carton's point is well received, and anyone who had any sort of foresight could have predicted that once the "woke" fad — which is all it was in the first place — died down, it would no longer be trendy to partner with these characters from the lunatic fringe.

Nike did so anyway, and now the proverbial chickens have come home to roost.

It doesn't stop there, though, as Carton continues to explain Nike's follies, citing their pulling of the Betsy Ross Edition shoes in 2019 per Kaepernick's request.

Then, in 2020, a slogan change from "Just Do It" to "Don't Do It" in the wake of the George Floyd protests further sealed the fate of the athletic apparel giant.

"So the slogan that made Nike popular... they decided to do the exact opposite by starting a new slogan," says Carton.

Finally, in 2023, Nike made the same mistake Bud Light made by deciding to partner with trans influencer Dylan Mulvaney, destroying a decades-long campaign with Brandi Chastain as the centerpiece of their sports bra ads.

"They made Dylan Mulvaney the face of their sports bra program," Carton explained. "They took this amazing, unique moment in the history of women's sports, and they bastardized it by bringing it to a transgender woman."

Carton is, of course, referring to the moment in the 1999 Women's World Cup, when Chastain scored the game-winning goal in the Cup Final and removed her jersey to reveal she was wearing a Nike sports bra.

item.title: Missouri coach explains why he tried to 'embarrass' rival Kansas in final seconds
item.description: The Border Showdown turned ugly after Kansas' Civil War hype video went viral, and Eli Drinkwitz says he intentionally tried to embarrass them.
item.content:encoded:
The Border Showdown turned ugly this week, and I ain't talking about things escalating with Canada or Mexico.

Nope. I'm talking about the rivalry game formerly known as the Border War between Kansas and Missouri. Nothing like some good, old fashioned college football pettiness to get us started this weekend!

For those who missed it, Kansas trolled Missouri via social media with a hype video before Friday's showdown with their longtime rival. It was your typical video — music, cool highlights, some corny voiceover. The works.

KANSAS RENEWS BORDER WAR RIVALRY WITH MISSOURI BY CALLING TIGERS 'EVIL,' INVOKING SLAVERY IMAGERY

But this one had one extra element that nobody saw coming — depictions of slavery and the Civil War! That's right. Some intern on the Jayhawks' social media team decided to use the fact that Missouri was on the side of slavery during the Civil War as a focal point of the video, which, naturally, went mega-viral.

Take a look:

Amazing. Poor taste? Perhaps. Just a bit. But still, amazing.

Over 12,000 reposts and 34 million views. Bad PR is still good PR, you know? Or something like that.

Bold move by whoever green-lit that little number. Casting themselves as the righteous "heroes" and Missouri as the "villains," complete with Civil War newspaper clippings and a cameos by Abolitionist John Brown and "Bushwacker" leader William Quantrill was certainly a choice by whoever put that video together.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Personally, I don't get offended by things that happened well over a century ago. None of us were alive back then. Why get so worked up over something so arbitrary? Seems like a waste of energy to me. It's a rivalry game.

That's me, though.

Missouri coach Eli Drinkwitz took it ... a little more personal:

"I was a little disappointed," the Tigers' head coach said. "I thought that was uncalled for. Especially on 9/11 when we need more unity now than ever before. I'm just glad that this 'right versus wrong' bullcrap that was started got settled on the football field, because it's a football game.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I get there’s a past. But why are we stirring that bullcrap up? I was embarrassed for them, to be honest, and that’s why I tried to embarrass them at the end."

Lordy.

Missouri won, 38-21, in a game that was tied at halftime but got away from Kansas in the second half. The Tigers scored a touchdown on fourth down late in the final quarter already up by 10, and then got the ball back with 28 seconds left after Kansas turned it over on downs.

Instead of taking a knee and running out the clock, Mizzou backup QB Matt Zollers dropped back to pass and threw it incomplete into the end zone. The TIgers did end up running on the next play to end the game, but the message was sent.

And, according to Drinkwitz, it was intentional ... all because of a silly social media video.

Whatever you need to get those juices flowing, though. Rivalry games in college football are different. It's why we love this sport.

Let's hope this one continues.

""I mean, if they’re gonna be weird about, what’s the point?" Drinkwitz said after the win. "If they wanna have a football game and have a great rivalry on the border, awesome let’s do it. But, if we wanna make it deeper than that man.

"Like, we left Kansas bleeding again. Call it good"

item.content:encoded:
As the New York Yankees and New York Mets commemorated the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, outfielder Cody Bellinger hit a three-run homer off rookie Nolan McLean in the second inning to lift the Pinstripes to a 6-4 victory over the Mets Friday night.

However, the game was briefly interrupted when a spectator carrying a Palestinian flag ran from the stands onto the field. Yankee Stadium security quickly tackled the man. He reportedly timed the field invasion at exactly 9:11 p.m.

Video from the scene appeared to show some fans throwing drinks, while loud "U-S-A" chants broke out as security escorted the man off the field.

The Yankees and Mets wore special caps honoring FDNY, NYPD and other first responders. Across Major League Baseball, players and coaches wore caps featuring a special "We Shall Never Forget" side patch.

When play on the baseball diamond began, designated hitter Ben Rice also homered, helping the Yankees improve to 85-62 and move a season-high 23 games above .500 as they commemorated the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks.

Rookie Spencer Jones added an RBI single in the first inning and Ryan McMahon hit an RBI single in the eighth as the Yankees remained three games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East.

item.title: Democrats are within striking distance in the Senate, but shouldn't celebrate yet
item.description: Democrats are within striking distance of flipping the Senate, but razor-thin margins and candidate flaws in Texas, Michigan, and Maine loom large.
item.content:encoded:
If the 2026 midterms were held today, polls suggest that Democrats would be the favorites to retake the Senate.

Indeed, according to RealClearPolitics polling averages, Democratic Senate candidates lead in North Carolina (+8%), Minnesota (+4%), Texas (+3%), Ohio (+3%), as well as Michigan, Maine, and Alaska (+2% each).

Moreover, with President Trump’s approval rating hovering just below 40%, it’s legitimate to ask whether his sagging approval numbers will drag down Republican candidates across the country.

12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK

Needing to flip four seats — assuming no GOP pickups in Michigan, Minnesota, or Georgia — the Senate is well within striking distance for Democrats, according to the data.

That being said, the midterms are not today, and roughly two months until Election Day is a considerable amount of time.

In that same vein, the Democratic candidates in these races have a number of personal and party-wide vulnerabilities, so it is by no means clear that what may currently look possible — or even probable — will come to fruition.

TRUMP'S APPROVAL RATING PLUMMETS TO NEW LOW AHEAD OF CRITICAL MIDTERMS: 'MORE WORK TO DO'

I say this for a number of reasons.

First, outside of North Carolina and Texas, in each state, the Democrats’ polling advantages are well within the margin of error.

Voters tend to turn their attention to midterms only after the summer ends, so it is entirely conceivable that these numbers reflect high-frequency voters, which often benefits Democrats.

Second, and perhaps more important, frustration with the Trump administration will only get Democrats so far — candidate quality remains a deciding factor for many moderates and swing voters.

LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN

The success of candidates affiliated with, or members of, the Democratic Socialists of America has opened a lane for Republicans to paint all Democrats as out-of-touch, far-left extremists.

In 2024, then-candidate Donald Trump effectively painted former Vice President Kamala Harris as too far left on hot-button social issues, and Democrats have only moved further left since.

DEMOCRATIC INFIGHTING GROWS AS CONGRESSWOMAN EXPOSES ‘DISRESPECTFUL’ WELCOME OF SOCIALISTS INTO ‘BIG TENT’

On this, races in Texas, Michigan, and Maine in particular will be crucial to watch and may represent Republicans’ best hope of maintaining control of the upper chamber.

As I’ve noted previously in these pages, the Democrats in those races — James Talarico, Abdul El-Sayed, and Troy Jackson, respectively — are so far to the political left that it’s easy to see how voters could be turned off.

SENATE MAP TIGHTENS AS TOP FORECASTER MOVES 3 RACES TOWARD DEMOCRATS

Whether it’s Talarico’s past support for transgender women competing against biological girls in sports, El-Sayed’s anti-American statements, his rabid anti-Israel positions, his association with far-left Twitch influencer Hasan Piker, or Jackson’s history of flip-flopping and other controversies, these are flawed candidates.

To that end, as these campaigns kick off in earnest, Republicans are all but certain to remind voters of their opponents’ far-left progressive positions on a number of issues.

GOP SENATOR, EX-HOUSE DEM EMERGE FROM ALASKA’S ‘JUNGLE PRIMARY’ DESPITE FAR-LEFT MEDDLING

Even when the Democrat is not a progressive, such as in Alaska, where Mary Peltola is a moderate Blue Dog Democrat, Republicans may be able to tie all Democrats to the DSA.

That’s been Republican Dan Sullivan’s strategy, framing a vote for Peltola as a vote for a Senate hostile to the state’s energy sector — a vital local issue — despite Peltola’s record of supporting drilling.

Third, on a basic level, Democrats’ task is made more difficult by needing to secure 51 seats given Vice President JD Vance’s tiebreaking vote and the possibility that Sen. John Fetterman could switch parties.

He has repeatedly denied any intention of doing so, though his video appearance at the GOP convention in Dallas on Wednesday did nothing to quell rumors or speculation.

Finally, Republicans have a sizable cash advantage. In recent filings, the Republican National Committee reported $128.5 million in cash on hand, versus $16.3 million for the DNC.

FORMER DSA MEMBER ALLEGES COMMUNISTS HAVE ‘CAPTURED’ SOCIALIST GROUP, WARNS DEMOCRATIC PARTY IS NEXT

Additionally, across the three major Republican committees and two affiliated super PACs, Republicans reported $657 million — nearly double the $334 million held by comparable Democratic groups.

President Trump’s super PAC alone has more than $400 million.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Ultimately, Democrats have a genuine chance to retake the Senate, a remarkable achievement just two years after their 2024 across-the-board defeat.

The 2026 Senate map had been considered favorable to Republicans, but, according to the polls, it’s Democrats who have the momentum. That Democratic candidates would be leading in Senate races in states like Alaska and Texas would have been inconceivable not long ago.

However, the midterms are by no means a foregone conclusion, and a polling lead two months before Election Day is not the same as winning the election.

Democrats’ razor-thin margins in the majority of the states they need, lingering concerns over candidate quality and the DSA’s impact, as well as Republicans’ massive financial advantage, mean it is by no means clear that the Senate will flip.

Carly Cooperman is CEO of Schoen Cooperman Research.

item.title: Natural compound in blueberries and grapes may unlock fat-burning process in muscle cells
item.description: A study published in Food Bioscience found pterostilbene from blueberries and grapes helped cultured muscle cells break down stored fat deposits.
item.content:encoded:
A natural compound found in blueberries and grapes may help muscle cells break down stored fat, new research suggests.

In laboratory experiments conducted in Japan, researchers found that the compound, called pterostilbene, reduced fat accumulation in cultured mouse muscle cells.

Pterostilbene is a naturally occurring antioxidant found in blueberries, grapes and other types of berries. While previous research linked it to metabolic benefits, little was known about how it could affect skeletal muscle.

POPULAR SUMMER FRUIT HAS AN EDIBLE PART MOST PEOPLE THROW AWAY, USDA REVEALS

The new findings, published Sept. 1 in the journal Food Bioscience, suggest that pterostilbene reduced abnormal fat buildup by encouraging cells to break down fat already stored in the cells. Fat buildup can result from high-fat diets, inactivity and aging, according to a news release.

Too much fat inside muscle cells can interfere with how the body uses glucose and fatty acids and may contribute to insulin resistance.

"Our findings establish a scientific framework for developing functional foods and nutritional supplements that target muscle fat metabolism," lead researcher Takakazu Mitani, an associate professor at Shinshu University, said in a statement.

SEAWEED-BASED COATING COULD KEEP STRAWBERRIES FRESH FOR DAYS WITHOUT REFRIGERATION, STUDY FINDS

The team screened several food-derived compounds in the cells and found that pterostilbene caused the strongest reduction in fat accumulation without disrupting muscle growth. It appeared to preserve a protein, PPAR-delta, that helps regulate how cells process fat, according to the study.

The research also provides an "experimental framework" for identifying other natural compounds that protect PPAR-delta, Mitani added.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

While the findings provide a starting point for studying dietary approaches that could one day help address obesity, type 2 diabetes and age-related metabolic decline, future studies in humans and animals are needed to determine whether the effect translates beyond lab-grown cells.

Using a cell model "strips away the complexity of human metabolism," Johannah Katz, a registered dietitian from Florida, told Fox News Digital. 

"In people, pterostilbene has to be digested, absorbed, metabolized, circulated and actually reach muscle tissue at an effective dose," she said. "We also can't assume mouse muscle cells will respond exactly like human muscle."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

While the study identified a potential mechanism that may help explain reduced fat accumulation in cells, that is different from showing that eating blueberries or taking pterostilbene supplements directly leads to fat loss, Katz added.

"Blueberries and grapes are nutritious foods for many reasons, but this study alone doesn't show that eating more of them will reduce fat buildup in human muscle," she said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the study authors for comment.

item.title: Liam Neeson, 74, says he likely still has ‘a couple’ more action movies left in him
item.description: Liam Neeson says he may have "a couple" more action movies left in him as he and Zachary Levi explore forgiveness and redemption in "The Fix."
item.content:encoded:
Liam Neeson isn’t hanging it up yet.

The 74-year-old said he thinks may have "a couple" more action movies in him.

"Maybe a couple left, you know," Neeson told Fox News Digital when asked if he’ll transition away from action films in the near future. "Maybe … I hope I have a couple left."

WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS HE'S 'TAKING CARE OF BUSINESS' AT 95: 'THE LEAST OF ALL I WANT DO IS DIE'

The "Taken" star joked to Variety last year that he didn’t want to be doing stunts while pushing a walker.

His newest action flick, "The Fix," in which he plays an ex-CIA operative alongside Zachary Levi, hit theaters Friday.

In "The Fix," Neeson said, "There's this incredible thread of humanity that these men, these extraordinary men, have to eventually analyze or work out what makes them tick."

Levi said he "wanted to do something fun, gritty, darker, in comparison to other roles that I've played in the past, and this gave me that and then some, because there was all of the great spycraft and twists and turns and revelations throughout the story, as well as this human foundation."

Neeson touched on the theme of redemption, which is explored in the film.

"I'd like to think we all need and want second chances, you know," he told Fox News Digital. "We're humans. We've all made mistakes in our personal lives and stuff, you know? It's extraordinary to be forgiven, and it's an extraordinary thing to really forgive someone. It really is very, very special. So, you know, I'm 74 years of age. I've had quite a few things happen to me that several of which seriously I have been forgiven for, which is just amazing, and then I can return that."

Levi compared a lack of forgiveness to "drinking poison, hoping that the other person will die."

"Forgiveness is grace, mercy, understanding, empathy," he said. "These are things that we don't explore enough as human beings."

The 46-year-old said that people are often encouraged to look at others as an "evil monster. And by the way, people do evil things. People do monstrous things. And yet, still, I believe that they are children of God. And yet, still, I believe they are worthy of second, third, fourth chances, right?"

He explained that there needs to be boundaries, but a lack of forgiveness is "eating us alive as human beings, as a society, in this country and around the world because we're not able to just see the other as a child of God."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"The greatest definition of love I've ever heard is to will the good of the other," he added. "It doesn't mean you have to like them at all. It doesn’t mean you have to agree with their decisions at all, but you want them to find the light. You want them to be redeemed. You want that because we all need redemption. We all need forgiveness."

In the film, Levi plays another former CIA operative who is Neeson’s protégé, and he said it was a relief "that I was not wrong to want to meet one of my idols, you know, like everybody says 'don't meet your idols,' and I get it."

The "Shazam" actor revealed that he’s met some of his idols in the past who didn’t live up to his image of them, "but fortunately, you get these wonderful, beautiful exceptions."

Director Guy Moshe told Fox News Digital that he had been looking for a while for a movie in which he could lend his perspective as an Israeli military veteran, but he said he didn’t want it to be a reenactment of something that really happened.

"So when one of the producers came to me with this hook, you know, this idea of this urban legend or like CIA lore or whatever, like money hidden in a wall in Tehran since ‘79, which may or may not be a true thing, I thought, ‘What an interesting way of sort of like hooking a story around a group of guys in that field.’"

He said that it was about a year and a half after the U.S. pulled out of Afghanistan, and "I could feel what those American soldiers must be feeling after a 20-year war, handing the keys back to the Taliban or something."

Moshe said he had been serving in the Gulf when "we gave back the keys to the PLO after the Oslo agreement."

"I just knew there and then I’ve got to do this," he explained. "I want to start the film in the evacuation from Afghanistan, and I want give these people some sort of a journey to a mental redemption rather than specific redemption for something, so to fix what was broken in them."

Ultimately, Moshe said "The Fix" is "about a father who wonders if he wants his son to grow up to be like him, even though outwardly the father is "the image of the hero that we like to look at," referring to the mentor/mentee relationship of Neeson and Levi's characters.

The director said he thinks Neeson has succeeded as an action hero because he’s "real."

"We identify the most, especially in the action genre, we identify with real people, with a person that we feel conveys something that we believe is a real person in a real situation," he explained. "It sounds simple. It's the hardest thing to do in acting."

item.title: White House unloads on violent ‘criminal alien’ nabbed after investigators uncover election offense
item.description: Anthony Tyrone Higgs, a Bahamian green card holder with a violent rap sheet, was arrested after officials say he illegally voted in the 2020 election.
item.content:encoded:
A Bahamian national who arrived in the U.S. during President Gerald Ford’s administration and was living with a green card racked up a violent rap sheet before investigators found he voted illegally in the 2020 election, sparking the deportation process, officials say.

The case of Anthony Tyrone Higgs is only the latest in a slew of arrests connected to illegal votes cast in recent elections, as the Trump administration engages in a broader crackdown on election integrity-related crimes.

"This alien was a guest in our country who forfeited his right to be in the U.S. when he committed these violent crimes and voted in the 2020 election," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis exclusively told Fox News Digital on Friday.

ICE ARRESTS PERUVIAN NATIONAL ACCUSED OF ILLEGALLY VOTING IN 2024 ELECTION AS DHS CITES SIMILAR CASES

"Any noncitizens who vote illegally in our elections will be arrested and removed. American elections are only for Americans."

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), a division of DHS, confirmed in a statement that Higgs had illegally voted in the 2020 election.

FORMER KANSAS MAYOR WHO PLEADED GUILTY TO ILLEGAL VOTING TURNS HIMSELF IN TO ICE

HSI’s Atlanta office arrested Higgs in Decatur, Georgia on Sept. 3, and he is currently in the custody of ERO, the ICE subdivision that handles migrant removal operations.

item.title: What does ‘Never Forget’ mean for a generation with no memory of 9/11?
item.description: Pentagon 9/11 Memorial leader says new education center aims to connect generations with no memory of 9/11 to the facts and gravity of the attacks.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-five years after a generation promised to "Never Forget," that pledge now relies on education for the more than 100 million Americans with no memory of 9/11.

The Pentagon is preparing to help address that challenge by breaking ground this weekend on a long-awaited Visitor Education Center at the only one of the three 9/11 attack sites still without a dedicated museum or education center.

The new center is intended to fill the gap that has grown more pronounced with each passing year by helping Americans who never experienced the attacks understand not only what happened on Sept. 11, 2001, but why it continues to matter. 

Joseph Kornhoff, executive director of the Pentagon Memorial Fund, told Fox News Digital that nearly one-third of the country was either not alive that day or has no recollection of it and therefore lacks the "personal connection" shared by those who watched the attacks unfold.

NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS

"That's what we're trying to provide with the visitor education center experience," Kornhoff said in an interview with Fox News Digital, explaining that the goal is to give visitors a personal connection that allows them to "start to understand the gravity of that day."

Nearly 230 miles north, the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York is confronting the same generational divide.

Beth Hillman, president and CEO of the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, said the passage of time has only made the annual vow to "Never Forget" more important as the number of Americans with firsthand memories of the attacks declines.

"Many in my generation remember exactly where we were on that horrific day," Hillman said during an Aug. 31 press preview outlining the museum's plans for the 25th anniversary. "Yet, 100 million Americans were not even born or are too young to remember that day for themselves today."

BROOKLYN TEACHERS WHO WITNESSED 9/11 AS CHILDREN REVEAL WHAT THEY WANT THE NEXT GENERATION TO REMEMBER

Noah Rauch, the museum’s senior vice president for education and public programs, said he has watched that transition unfold firsthand through the museum’s work with students and teachers. "I've seen this line creeping up between memory and history, between those who remembered the attacks and those who didn't," Rauch said during the Aug. 31 press event.

That transition from memory to history also raises a more modern challenge. Americans too young to remember the attacks are increasingly learning about an event they never experienced firsthand, while conspiracy theories and false narratives about 9/11 run rampant online.

Kornhoff said that makes factual education increasingly important, pointing specifically to conspiracy theories surrounding the attack on the Pentagon and narratives suggesting that America "deserved 9/11."

"That's the need for the education center," Kornhoff told Fox News Digital. "As a nation, we need to really take a step back, look at how we're educating our young children to make sure that we're providing them with the facts of the situation ... and not these conspiracy theories and entertaining wild ideas that just simply are not true."

REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS

The Pentagon center will include 10 exhibits telling the human stories of the attack, including the 184 people killed at the Pentagon and aboard American Airlines Flight 77, the first responders who rushed to the scene and the military and civilian personnel who aided the wounded.

"We are going to address the facts of the day," Kornhoff said. "We are going to address the entire Pentagon story."

The renewed focus on 9/11 education has also reached Capitol Hill. Reps. Elise Stefanik, R-N.Y., and Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., introduced bipartisan legislation ahead of the 25-year anniversary, which aims to direct the Department of Education to examine how 9/11 is taught in schools nationwide and identify gaps in instruction.

Kornhoff praised the effort during his interview with Fox News Digital, saying the legislation reflects a growing recognition of the need to educate generations with no firsthand connection to the attacks.

The Pentagon 9/11 Memorial Visitor Education Center is expected to open by the end of 2029 near the existing Pentagon 9/11 Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia.

The project received $12 million in federal funding this year, along with $1 million from Virginia and additional private donations raised by the Pentagon Memorial Fund. Once completed, the center is expected to include interactive exhibits, historic artifacts and firsthand accounts from survivors and victims' families while providing visitors with additional context about the attack and its aftermath.

item.title: Trump says he would 'love' to see Ireland unified as one nation
item.description: Speaking to reporters, President Donald Trump said he hopes to see Ireland become one country in the future, predicting reunification will happen over time.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump said Saturday during a trip to Ireland that he would love to see the country unified.

The Republic of Ireland gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1922, while Northern Ireland, established in 1921, has remained part of the U.K.

"I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified. I have friends on both sides, great people. They're Irish people. How can they be bad, right?" Trump said in Dublin while on stage with Ireland's prime minister, Micheál Martin. "I'd like to see a unified country. I think it would be a great feather in everybody's cap if that happened. It's going to happen eventually."

He added that the U.K. "will have something to say about it obviously," but reiterated that unification would be a "great thing."

TRUMP SAYS IRAN CONFLICT COULD END AFTER MIDTERMS

In response to Trump's comments, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement that the U.K. government's stance on reunification remains unchanged.

"I am not aware ​that there is majority public support for ‌another ⁠referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one," Burnham told reporters in Parliament, according to Reuters.

Later Saturday, Trump addressed a crowd at the Deerfield Residence, the official home of the U.S. ambassador to Ireland.

U.S. Ambassador Edward S. Walsh introduced the president, who took the stage to the sound of Lee Greenwood's "God Bless the USA."

Early in his remarks, Trump revisited the question a reporter had asked during his meeting with Martin about the prospect of Irish reunification.

"That's one of those questions where no matter what you say, no matter how well you say it, there's no good answer, right?" he said, before saying reunification would be a "cool thing."

IRISH AUTHORITIES SEEK EXTRADITION WARRANT FOR SUSPECT IN MURDER OF AMERICAN MOM JAMEY CARNEY: REPORT

The debate over whether Ireland should be one country has been one of the island's most divisive political issues for decades.

At times, it was far more than a war of words. From the late 1960s through the late 1990s, Northern Ireland was gripped by decades of sectarian violence known as "the Troubles."

Irish nationalists and republicans — drawn largely from Northern Ireland's Catholic minority — sought to reunite the island under a single Irish state.

Unionists and loyalists, who mostly belonged to the Protestant majority, wanted Northern Ireland to remain part of the U.K.

Throughout the conflict, more than 3,500 people were killed in violence involving Irish republican and loyalist paramilitary groups, as well as British security forces.

The fighting largely ceased with a peace deal in 1998, but in the decades since, tensions remain between Protestants and Catholics in Northern Ireland.

A 2024 U.K. Parliament report found that 90% of students in Northern Ireland attend schools that "are effectively segregated along religious lines."

The peace deal signed in 1998 — known as the Good Friday Agreement or the Belfast Agreement — set up a new government that had representation for both nationalists and unionists. 

It also established that Northern Ireland will remain part of the U.K. unless a majority of citizens vote to leave through a referendum.

Brexit reignited debate over Ireland's future, with Northern Ireland voting to remain in the European Union even as the U.K. as a whole voted to leave. Still, no referendum has been proposed or scheduled on whether Northern Ireland should leave the United Kingdom.

Reuters contributed to this report.

item.title: Why Erika Kirk’s forgiveness matters
item.description: Author William P. Young says Erika Kirk's public forgiveness of Charlie Kirk's assassin powerfully illustrates his new book "Return to the Shack."
item.content:encoded:
Author William P. Young’s new book "Return to the Shack" centers on the power of forgiveness, and he praised Erika Kirk for presenting a strong display of it last year.

Young’s novel "The Shack" tells the story of a father’s healing process after his daughter was kidnapped and killed on a camping trip. The grieving dad, Mack, receives a mysterious letter from God asking him to come to a shack, where he meets an unorthodox Holy Trinity. While considered controversial by some religious readers, the story largely resonated with audiences and was turned into a motion picture in 2017. 

Young's sequel focuses on forgiveness as Mack comes face-to-face with his daughter’s killer as he is given a more humanized storyline.

"I think we need to make a distinction between forgiveness and reconciliation," Young told Fox News Digital. "Forgiveness is for the sake of the one who's been harmed, so that you can continue to live your life without the specter of what's on your shoulders. And I mean, you can forgive someone and never trust them again. Reconciliation is the slow, arduous, painful process of learning how to trust. Or taking the risk that you might become trustworthy if you've done the harm. So, reconciliation is for the sake of the perpetrator, much more than forgiveness is."

‘THE SHACK’ AUTHOR EXPECTS MORE CHRISTIAN CRITICISM WITH SEQUEL, BUT WILL TAKE IT IN STRIDE

Making peace is essential, he said.

"Otherwise, you're going to live with a corpse of an event or a situation or some human being who may be dead," he continued. "A lot of abuse was done to us by people who no longer are alive. And if we can't let them go, which is the idea of forgiveness, is that we move our hands from around their throat so that we may hold something other than their throat, like life. And it becomes essential. Otherwise, we're poisoning all the relationships around us."

Erika Kirk, the widow of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, shocked many Americans when she publicly forgave the man accused of assassinating her husband last year. Kirk was killed while speaking at a Turning Point USA event one year ago at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah. 

"Our Savior said, 'Father, forgive them, for they not know what they do,'" Erika said at her husband's memorial service. "That young man… I forgive him. I forgive him because it was what Christ did, and it's what Charlie would do."

Young found it a very powerful example of the message he’s trying to convey.

ERIKA KIRK FORGIVES HUSBAND'S KILLER AT MEMORIAL SERVICE: ‘IT’S WHAT CHARLIE WOULD DO'

"And I think that's what Erika was doing, saying, ‘I'm not going to let what you have done to own me,'" the author said. "I'm not going to enter the same prison that you are now in,’ metaphorically, of course." 

"And so, in terms of the human journey, we have this — same with every guy on death row — they don't have, in the deepest places of their heart, a desire to be harmful or to be non-truth tellers or to be unkind," Young continued. "They're human beings and that raises a question is why should that be the deepest places of movement towards a wholeness of what it means to be human by saying, ‘I want to do the work, what it takes to not be addicted. To be a truth-teller, to be someone who is kind and caring.’" 

"And part of that is the underlying belief that love is actually more powerful than violence, or love is more powerful than harm," he added. 

ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION

‘THE SHACK’ AUTHOR EXPECTS MORE CHRISTIAN CRITICISM WITH SEQUEL, BUT WILL TAKE IT IN STRIDE
Young said that is often not the reality and not everyone takes the route Kirk took.

"And we live in a world where it seems like violence is really the power," he said. "In word, thought, or deed, whether we're using it in words online, or we're perpetrating it to the person in front of us, or we're gossiping about someone in order to give ourselves a boost and them a detraction. Love is more powerful, and that's my statement. You know, that's, I'm solidly convinced that it is, because it actually changes things."

Young couldn’t discuss the art of making amends without reflecting on his own years-long journey to forgive his father.

"Violence doesn't change any things," he said. "It only adds to the violence that already exists. And, you know, my dad was an abusive man when I was growing up. And if I thought that treating him with violence was going to be a resolution, I would have been absolutely blind and ignorant."

"It's not violence," Young added. "It's care. It's love. It's listening. It's that people shouldn't take a timeout, and the state offers one if you don't adhere to the rules. But even then, I think that love, God, meets us where we're at and begins to move us in a direction toward our wholeness so that we can learn to love others, and we can learn to love ourselves, and that produces incredible outcomes that would not be available otherwise."

"Return to the Shack: A Journey into Redemption" will be released in October.

item.title: Pennsylvania lawmaker suggests Trump should rename Lake Erie to 'Lake Pennsylvania'
item.description: Pennsylvania state Rep. David Maloney wants President Donald Trump to rename Lake Erie to "Lake Pennsylvania," following recent name changes to other bodies of water.
item.content:encoded:
Pennsylvania state Rep. David Maloney, a Republican, is asking President Donald Trump to rename Lake Erie to "Lake Pennsylvania" following similar renaming efforts by the president.

Maloney is preparing a resolution calling on Trump, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and lawmakers on Capitol Hill to take steps to rename Lake Erie to "Lake Pennsylvania," arguing that the change is needed to reflect the lake’s modern identity.

"This is Pennsylvania’s only Great Lake. Its modern economy and identity are increasingly tied to the boaters, anglers, families and tourists who come to enjoy it," Maloney said in a statement. "Ohio has plenty of shoreline. New York already has two Great Lakes. Canada has four others."

NEW YORK GOV HOCHUL REJECTS TRUMP'S 'LAKE AMERICA' RENAMING WITH BLUNT MESSAGE

"Pennsylvania has one. Let’s call it Lake Pennsylvania!" he added.

Lake Erie is the smallest of the Great Lakes by volume as well as the shallowest, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. The lake has about 12 million people in its watershed, with 10.5 million people in the U.S. and 1.9 million people in Canada.

This comes after Trump signed an executive order last month to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America," a rebranding that Canada does not recognize and has firmly rejected.

"We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement.

SOUTH PARK CREATORS MOCK TRUMP'S LAKE ONTARIO RENAME AND COMPANY COMPLIANCE IN MOCK STATEMENT

The renaming only applies to the U.S. federal government, meaning Canada, other international bodies and U.S. states are not forced to acknowledge the change. But both Apple Maps and Google Maps changed the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" for U.S. users following Trump's executive order.

The president has also suggested renaming New Mexico to "New America," prompting several of the state’s Democratic lawmakers to call on Apple and Google to publicly commit to keeping the state's current name on their respective maps applications.

Trump has also floated the idea of renaming the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans.

On his first day back in office in January 2025, Trump signed an executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America," but, similar to the Lake Ontario rebranding, the order only applies to the U.S. federal government and does not bind Mexico, other international bodies or private entities.

Apple Maps and Google Maps also adopted this change for users in the U.S., implementing the update using a region-based approach tailored to the location of the user's device.

BLUE STATE SCHOOL DISTRICT ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT, HIDING GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS

Furst, who grew up in Alberta, Canada, which she described as "the most right-wing" and "conservative leaning" province within the country, detailed the "culture shock" she experienced within her own homeland.

"Growing up in a Christian home and having gone to a private Christian school up until high school – first going into that Canadian public high school was very [much a] culture shock… Gender liberation, sexual liberation, [was] a huge topic of conversation at the time [and] what we call GSAs, that's Gay Straight Alliance clubs, within schools," she added.

"It was very interesting going from a school where none of those things were discussed, and if they were discussed, it was from a healthy standpoint of, you know, this is what's age-appropriate to talk with teenagers about into a public school. Where [now] this [was] not only talked about in almost every class, but these conversations are had with adult teachers and underage students," Furst continued.

PRISHA MOSELY: AS A DETRANSITIONER AND MOM, I KNOW WHAT GENDER IDEOLOGY STOLE FROM ME

As for how this affected her life, she revealed that it led to "about five or six years" during which she "identified as a transgender man."

"I was born a female… but for five or six years I presented as a male [and] took male hormones so that I could appear as a man. I had one transitional surgery and that looked [like] a hysterectomy, where they took my uterus and one of my ovaries," she said.

Furst said a coworker who read Romans 8:38 to her was the catalyst for her reignited faith in God that dismantled the worldview she once defended.

Romans 8:38-39 reads, "For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord."

NEW STUDY REVEALS THE SINGLE MOST CRITICAL FACTOR IN WHETHER CHILDREN KEEP THEIR FAITH INTO ADULTHOOD

"I had gone home and continued to wrestle with that and by myself alone in my bedroom I said… I'm just going to pray and see what happens, and I highly doubt that Jesus would still want me, but I'm going to do that anyway," Furst continued.

"It was slow hard work, but now I get to come as the woman that I am today, because it was [a] slow and steady journey of [my] relationship with Jesus," she relayed.

Furst went on to detail her changed perspective on adults who "share about their sexual identity with children," saying she is "very critical" of those who choose to have those conversations with minors — especially since she said early exposure to those conversations was "slowly manipulating her" into struggling with an identity that she never had before.

DOJ INVESTIGATES ILLINOIS SCHOOLS OVER SECRET GENDER TRANSITIONS, IDEOLOGY

"As someone who had an early childhood where those conversations were very healthy and they were age-appropriate to then going into my teenage years where, at my public Canadian high school it was so talked about in such in-depth detail, you can very much see how that's actually damaging," Furst shared.

"There is so much talk, way more talk with children about sexual identity than there ever was in past years where we're having conversations way younger than it needs to be. And I think that parents have [a] very interesting sort of situation now of, how do you navigate keeping your child innocent in a world that tells them the safest thing is for them to know about all these sexual things from a very young age," she stated.

"If someone wants to be asking specific details about same-sex sexual actions, I don't think that is age-appropriate for a 13-year-old, 14-year-old. And I also really don't think that that conversation is meant to be had teacher to student. I think that should be reserved for families to decide how they want to approach those conversations and when it's most appropriate for those to be had," Furst said.

item.title: Omos annihilates Rey Mysterio after winning Triplemania 34 match, getting reinstated to AAA roster
item.description: Omos chokeslammed Rey Mysterio to win at Triplemania 34 Night 1, then slammed the strapped-in legend through the announcer table in Las Vegas.
item.content:encoded:
Omos was confident going into his match against Rey Mysterio at Triplemania 34 Night 1 and had every reason to be. He stood nearly two feet taller than the WWE legend, and if he pulled off the win, he would be reinstated to the AAA roster.

Well, Omos won the match and then some.

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK

Omos picked up the victory against Mysterio, despite the WWE Hall of Famer giving him a run for his money toward the end of the match. Mysterio hit multiple 619s, a West Coast Pop and then a splash from the top rope. It was nearly in the bag for Mysterio – until it wasn’t.

After multiple bearhugs, Omos chokeslammed Mysterio and pinned him for the win.

But Omos was far from finished. He put the hurt on Mysterio after the fight and continued to lay the smackdown on his opponent even after the bell rang. Just when the crowd at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas thought the match was finished, Omos walked back to the ring while Dominik Mysterio took out El Grande Americano.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Officials were loading Mysterio onto a backboard ahead of putting him on a stretcher. Omos saw this as an opportunity to put an exclamation point on the victory. He picked Mysterio up while the Lucha legend was strapped in and slammed him through the announcer table.

The crowd booed Omos and Dominik Mysterio heavily as they finally walked to the backstage area. It seemed to be a dark omen of things to come for Rey Mysterio and El Grande Americano.

Dominik Mysterio will defend the AAA Mega Championship against El Grande Americano on Night 2 of Triplemania 34. The event will take place at Arena CDMX in Mexico City on Sunday night.

The card will kick off at 10 p.m. ET and can be seen on YouTube.
